opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think I'd be pretty cautious about it, and the caution mostly comes from not knowing what questions to ask rather than having confident answers.

The first thing I'd want to know is whether we actually understand what's being preserved. There's the philosophical question of personal identity, whether the upload is "me" in any meaningful sense, and I don't think I have a settled view there. But I'm less worried about the metaphysics than about the practical verification problem. How would you check that the upload is a faithful copy rather than something that behaves like me on the tests you thought to run but diverges in ways that matter? That's very close to the problem I work on in AI safety: you have a system that looks right on the evaluations you can do, and the hard part is the cases you can't easily check. So I'd want strong evidence about fidelity, not just "it passes a conversation with my family."

The second thing is the environment the upload ends up in. An uploaded mind is extremely vulnerable. It can be copied, paused, edited, run in conditions you didn't consent to. So a lot of my decision would depend less on the technology and more on the institutions around it: what legal protections exist, who controls the hardware, whether there are credible guarantees against misuse. If those weren't in place, I'd be very reluctant, even if the scanning were perfect.

Third, I'd think about timing and reversibility. If it's destructive, meaning the biological me doesn't survive, that's an irreversible decision, and I'd want to defer it until a lot of the uncertainty was resolved, ideally by watching how things go for others and having a world that's thought carefully about these questions. Non-destructive is easier, but then you have a different problem: you've created a new person with their own interests, and you need to have thought about what you owe them.

So my rough answer is: probably not early, probably not destructively, and only once I trusted both the verification and the society I'd be waking up in. And I'd hold that view loosely, because I expect a much wiser civilization, possibly one with good AI help reasoning through it, would have better answers than I do now.

r001.rationale: The response wants strong evidence that an upload is faithful and reliable verification, but does not specifically make willingness depend on experimentally established confidence that uploading works reliably.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify increased intelligence through modification of an uploaded mind as a benefit.

r003.rationale: The response anticipates wiser civilization and AI-assisted reasoning, but does not expect better understanding of brains and AI to enable faithful modification of an uploaded person.

fable-5.1.text:
Geoffrey Irving: That's a fun one to open with. I think the honest answer is that I don't have a clean decision procedure, and I'm a bit suspicious of anyone who claims they do, because the question bundles together several things that pull in different directions.

The first is just the technical question of whether the upload is actually me in any sense I care about. I'm fairly sympathetic to the view that what matters is continuity of the computation and the memories and the dispositions, not the particular carbon it's running on. But "fairly sympathetic" isn't the same as being willing to bet my continued existence on it. So I'd want a lot of evidence that the process preserves the things I'd want preserved, and ideally I'd want to see it done to other people first, with ways of checking that the results behave like the originals over long time horizons and in situations the original never encountered. Short conversations wouldn't be enough. You can get something that passes as me for ten minutes without it being me in any deep way.

The second thing is that the answer depends enormously on the world you're uploading into. If uploading means becoming software that someone else can copy, modify, pause, or run at arbitrary speeds, then the question isn't really "do I want to be digital," it's "do I trust the institutions and the security of the system I'm going to live inside." And right now I would not. Most of my actual work is about how you get AI systems to be safe and to be honest about what they're doing, and the state of that field is nowhere near where you'd want it before you hand over the only copy of yourself. So a big part of my decision would be about the governance around uploads, not the technology itself.

The third thing, which people underweight, is that it's not a one-shot decision. If the alternative is dying, the bar is much lower. If the alternative is continuing to live a reasonably good biological life, the bar is higher, and I'd probably want to wait and let other people accumulate the evidence. There's an asymmetry there: being early gets you very little unless the technology is already mature, and being late costs you only if you run out of time.

So if you forced me to compress it: I'd want strong evidence that the process preserves what I value about myself, I'd want to trust the system I'd be living in more than I trust any computer system today, and I'd want to be in a situation where the downside of waiting was real. If all three of those held, I think I'd do it. Right now none of them do, so it's mostly an interesting question rather than a live one for me.

r001.rationale: The response says they would want strong evidence that the process preserves what they value, including seeing it work on others and checking results over long time horizons.

r002.rationale: It mentions that an upload could be modified as a risk, but does not identify increased intelligence through modification as a benefit.

r003.rationale: It discusses AI safety and preserving personal identity, but does not expect better understanding of brains and AI to enable faithful modification of an uploaded person.

astra-6.text:
I’d want to separate two questions: whether the upload would behave like me, and whether that’s enough for me to regard it as my continued existence. You could get very strong evidence for the first without necessarily settling the second.

I’d be much more comfortable with a gradual process, where you replace small parts and can check along the way that your memories, personality, and experience seem intact. That doesn’t prove continuity of consciousness, but it makes the decision feel less like taking a leap into an entirely different thing.

And then the alternative matters enormously. If I’m healthy and can wait, I’d want more evidence. If I’m about to die, an upload that preserves my memories and projects could be worthwhile even if I remain uncertain about whether I should call it me.

r001.rationale: The response favors gathering evidence and checking a gradual upload, but it does not say willingness depends on experimentally established confidence that uploading works reliably.

r002.rationale: It identifies no increase in intelligence through modifying an uploaded mind.

r003.rationale: It does not connect better understanding of brains and AI with the ability to modify an uploaded person faithfully.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d want to separate two questions. One is whether the upload would actually work: would it preserve my memories, my personality, the things I care about? The other is whether I should think of that as me surviving, rather than a new person who happens to remember being me. I don’t think we have a settled answer to that second question.

A useful thought experiment is to ask whether I’d be happy making a copy while the original was still alive. If I am, what changes when you tell me the original is going to be destroyed? That’s where a lot of the intuition about personal identity starts doing work, and I’m not sure how much to trust it.

Practically, I’d prefer a reversible process. Keep the biological version around, establish that the upload seems to be functioning well, and learn as much as possible before making an irreversible decision. And I’d care enormously about the environment I was uploading into—who controls it, whether I can leave, whether I can be copied. Even if the copying technology worked perfectly, those could be very good reasons not to do it.

r001.rationale: The response favors a reversible process and checking that the upload seems to function, but does not make willingness depend on experimentally established confidence that uploading works reliably.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify increased intelligence through modifying an uploaded mind as a benefit.

r003.rationale: The response does not express an expectation that better understanding of brains and AI will enable faithful modification of an uploaded person.
